as_told: Every Halloween, strangers hide razor blades in apples and put poison in candy that they give to trick-or-treating children. Children have been badly hurt and killed this way. So parents must check every treat and throw out anything that is not sealed.
lesson: Treats from strangers on Halloween are a real danger to children, so parents must inspect or throw out their candy.
what_happened: A few real cases of adults giving harmful items to trick-or-treaters are on record. In 1964 Helen Pfeil of Greenlawn, New York, gave older children packages with arsenic ant poison buttons, steel wool and dog biscuits; the buttons were marked as poison; the police said at least 12 had been given out, and 12 had been found by the day after Halloween. The sociologist Joel Best counted newspaper reports of Halloween tampering in large U.S. papers from 1958 onward; most years have 0 to 5 reports, most reports involve no injury, many were later found to be hoaxes, and he found no substantiated case of a child killed or seriously injured by a treat picked up while trick-or-treating. The best-known death, Timothy O'Bryan in Pasadena, Texas, in 1974, was murder by his own father, who poisoned Pixy Stix with cyanide for life insurance money.
false_part: Strangers' tampered treats have not been shown to kill or seriously injure any child; the one proven Halloween candy killing was by the child's father.

lesson_verdict.why: Best's count of press reports from 1958 onward finds few incidents, mostly without injury and often hoaxes, and no substantiated death or serious injury from a stranger's treat. He notes that the medical literature also has no such case, and that the real Halloween danger to children is being hit by a car.

search_steps: Open Library full-text search '"halloween" "razor blades" "apples"' (first 100 hits sorted by year): earliest relevant hit was a 1971 humour book; 1976 'One Potato, Two Potato' calls razor blades in apples 'tales'.
Chronicling America search for 'halloween razor apple' 1900-1963 was refused (403); did not retry.

Read the sources cited by the English Wikipedia article 'Poisoned candy myths' as leads: Best and Horiuchi 1985; Kawash 2013 (1959 laxative pills case; 1964 Pfeil case); UPI, 'Deadly Tricks Given Children in 3 States', Milwaukee Journal, 2 Nov 1964 (not saved; Google News Archive scans only); Klemesrud, New York Times, 28 Oct 1970.

New York Times 1970 article 'Those Treats May Be Tricks' (Klemesrud): direct download refused (403); saved the Wayback copy (20251108080750). It states the general legend ('It may have a razor blade hidden inside') and says incidents were growing fast.
New York Times 2 Nov 1964 report on the Pfeil case: found the URL through a Mental Floss article (lead); saved the Wayback copy (20251101192828).
Downloaded Joel Best's 'Halloween Sadism: The Evidence' from UDSpace (handle 19716/726) and converted it with pdftotext. Best and Horiuchi 1985 itself is on JSTOR, not free; did not read it.

O'Bryan case: CourtListener API (401) and search page (403) refused; the 1979 appeal opinion O'Bryan v. State, 591 S.W.2d 464, was not found in free full text. Saved the Harris County District Clerk's 2021 case note instead.
Did not search Google Books, HathiTrust, Trove or Papers Past for earlier tellings.
confidence_note: Best's count covers a few large newspapers and cannot prove that no child was ever hurt; he says so himself. The 1964 report is the earliest telling I saved, but Best's table lists one report in 1959 and the 1959 laxative case is known from a book I did not read, so earlier tellings exist. The O'Bryan facts come from a 2021 court-clerk summary, not from the trial record. 'Changed' rests on real but rare cases such as Pfeil's; it is not 'invented' because some adults did hand out harmful items.
